validator: draft 1 passed with no hard or soft problems. The faults below are the critic's.
keep: The idea is named up front in two plain sentences: one part seen square-on from several sides, set out by a fixed rule, so you can rebuild it in your head.
The causal step is there: looking square-on, every point along the line of sight lands on one spot, so each view keeps two sizes and loses one. That is why several views are needed (screen 2).
The glass box gives the cause of each view's place: the wall it is cast onto, then the box opened flat. First angle first, third angle beside it, and the symbol that says which.

Fourteen screens alternate SHOW and DO, ending on three mixed puzzles (12, 13, 14). Each misconception in the brief has a DO screen with its own hint: views placed by the wrong rule (4, 6), the 3D shape not seen from the views (14, which needs two views together), a hidden edge read as visible (8), a cut rib hatched (10).
Screen 8 asks for a paper sketch, then compares it with the drawn view after Check.
Only the tolerance limit and the drawn length are figures, so they are the only typed answers, each with its slips. Everything else is a direction, a named part or a description.

Only two sources reach this idea, and both are cited where they support the words. The line types, hatching and the rib rule are textbook-standard drawing conventions, stated plainly; the fact-checker should confirm them against the UW, MIT and LibreTexts quotes in the brief's notes 2.2.
fix: Causal step skipped: the explain names the projection symbol but never says how to read it. Add that in first angle the cone's wide end faces the circles, and in third angle its narrow end does.

Misconception not shown failing in the explain: say what goes wrong when a sheet is read by the wrong rule. The view from the left is taken as the view from the right, and the part comes out mirrored.
Brief shows the effect, not the cause: it names the views landing in place but not why. Say each view is carried on the wall it is drawn on.
False absolute: 'one view always hides a size. Never judge a feature from a single view.' Say a single square-on view hides one size, so judge a feature from at least two.
Overclaim: 'The title block holds the scale, the units ...'. Title blocks differ. Say it usually holds them.
Screen 4's hint names third angle before screen 5 teaches it. Say the near side instead.
Talks about the lessons, not the idea: 'Every diagram so far mapped what is joined to what.' Say a schematic maps what is joined to what, and an engineering drawing is different.
Analogy muddled: a wall elevation 'not how far into the room the wall is' means nothing for a socket. The plan gives where along the wall, the elevation gives how high.

Unreadable labels: three views, the turnable bracket and the symbol will not fit at 340 px, and screen 5 puts two whole sheets side by side. Once unfolded, shrink the bracket to a small turnable copy above the sheet; at phone width stack the two sheets one above the other; keep the projection symbol at least 40 px wide.
Screen 11 starts a sentence with a numeral. Write 'A size of 25 ± 0.1 means ...'.
'Cast onto the wall beyond the part' is hard to picture. Add 'behind the part, on the far side from you' where it first appears.
